title: Asynchronous FIFO
summary: Passes data safely between two unrelated clocks, using Gray-code pointers and 2-flip-flop synchronizers. A favourite interview question.
how: Writes happen on wclk and reads on rclk. The data sits in a shared memory.
Each side keeps its own pointer, with one extra bit so that full and empty can be told apart.
Pointers cross to the other clock domain in Gray code, where only one bit changes at a time, through two flip-flops.
Empty: the read pointer has caught up with the write pointer. Full: the top two Gray bits differ and the rest match.
A simulator cannot show metastability, so passing the testbench does not prove the clock crossing is safe in hardware. For real chips, run CDC checks and constrain the crossing paths.
diagram:
WRITE side (wclk)                          READ side (rclk)
  wdata ───────────►[  dual-clock memory  ]───────────► rdata
  winc ──► write pointer ──► Gray ──► [FF][FF] ──► empty? ◄── read pointer ◄── rinc
  wfull ◄── full? ◄── [FF][FF] ◄── Gray ◄── read pointer
try: Change ASIZE to 4 (16 entries). The testbench uses DEPTH = 8, so update DEPTH and the .ASIZE value in it too.
expect: PASS: async_fifo, 3064 items crossed between two clocks in order (full and empty both exercised)

title: Synchronous FIFO
summary: A first-in, first-out queue on a single clock, with full, empty and count flags.
how: A memory plus a write pointer and a read pointer.
The pointers have one extra bit: equal means empty, same address but different top bit means full.
Writes when full and reads when empty are ignored.
expect: PASS: sync_fifo, 4000 random cycles (full 1276 times, empty 1293 times)

title: Dual-port RAM
summary: One write port and one read port with a registered read, the style FPGA tools turn into block RAM.
how: Writing happens on the clock edge when we is 1.
The read data appears one clock after the address.
Reading and writing the same address in the same cycle returns the old value.
try: Make a single-port version that shares one address for reading and writing.
expect: PASS: ram, 2000 random reads and writes

title: 4-to-1 multiplexer
summary: Chooses one of four inputs. The most basic building block.
how: A case statement picks the input named by sel.
Every case gives y a value, so no unwanted latch is created.

title: Ripple-carry adder
summary: An adder built from 1-bit full adders with generate, showing how bigger circuits are made from small ones.
how: A full adder adds two bits and a carry.
generate creates one full adder per bit and chains their carries.
It is simple but slow for wide numbers, because the carry travels through every bit.
try: Replace the generate block with a single 'assign {cout, sum} = a + b + cin;' and compare the Yosys cell counts.

title: 7-segment decoder
summary: Shows a hex digit (0 to F) on a 7-segment display.
how: A lookup table written as a case statement.
seg is ordered g,f,e,d,c,b,a and 1 means the segment is on.
try: Add a 'blank' input that turns all segments off.

title: ALU
summary: Eight operations (add, subtract, logic, shifts and compare) with carry and zero flags. The calculator inside a CPU.
how: op selects the operation.
The extra bit on add and subtract becomes the carry or borrow.
zero is 1 when the result is 0.
try: Add an arithmetic right shift (keeps the sign bit) as a new operation.

title: Up/down counter
summary: A counter with reset, load, enable and direction control.
how: Reset has the highest priority, then load, then counting.
It wraps around naturally at both ends.
try: Make it stop at a MAX value instead of wrapping.

title: Universal shift register
summary: Holds, shifts left, shifts right or loads in parallel. Used to turn serial data into parallel and back.
how: mode selects hold, shift right, shift left or load.
ser_msb and ser_lsb are the bits that enter at each end.
try: Add a rotate mode where the bit that falls off comes back in at the other end.

title: Edge detector
summary: Gives a one-clock pulse when a signal rises or falls.
how: It remembers the signal from the previous clock.
Comparing old and new values shows which edge happened.
The input must already be synchronous to the clock.
try: Add a 2-flip-flop synchronizer in front, so it can take a signal from outside the chip.

title: Button debouncer
summary: Cleans up a bouncing mechanical button so that one press counts once.
how: Two flip-flops synchronize the button.
The output changes only after the input has stayed different for STABLE_CYCLES clocks.
Any bounce back restarts the timer.
try: Connect it to the edge detector to get one pulse per button press.
expect: PASS: debouncer, 3 bouncy presses gave exactly 3 clean changes

title: Clock divider (tick generator)
summary: Makes slow events from a fast clock, using a clock-enable tick.
how: A counter runs from 0 to DIV-1.
tick pulses once every DIV clocks. Use it as an enable, not as a new clock.
try: Use tick as the enable of the counter design to count once per second.
expect: PASS: clock_divider, 100 ticks exactly 5 clocks apart

title: PWM generator
summary: Pulse width modulation for dimming LEDs and controlling motors.
how: A free-running counter is compared with duty.
The output is high for duty out of every 256 clocks (8-bit).
try: Slowly sweep duty up and down to make an LED 'breathe'.
expect: PASS: pwm, high time equals duty for 12 settings

title: Sequence detector FSM (1011)
summary: A Moore state machine that finds 1011 in a stream of bits, including overlapping matches.
how: Each state means how much of 1011 has been seen.
One block stores the state, another works out the next state.
The SystemVerilog version uses a typedef enum for readable states.
try: Change it to detect 1101. Draw the state diagram first. You will also need to change the pattern in the testbench.
expect: PASS: sequence_detector, found 1011 181 times with no mistakes

title: Round-robin arbiter
summary: Lets several requesters share one resource fairly by taking turns.
how: x & (~x + 1) keeps only the lowest 1 bit.
A mask gives priority to requesters above the last winner.
If nobody above is asking, it wraps around to the lowest requester.
try: Set N = 8 and update the testbench to match.
expect: PASS: round_robin_arbiter, 2473 fair grants, nobody waited more than 3 turns

title: UART transmitter
summary: Sends bytes over a serial line (8N1), as used to talk to a computer.
how: The line idles high. A frame is a start bit, 8 data bits (lowest first) and a stop bit.
CLKS_PER_BIT sets the baud rate: clock frequency divided by baud rate.
A 4-state machine steps through the frame.
try: Add an even parity bit before the stop bit.
expect: PASS: uart_tx, 50 bytes decoded correctly from the serial line

title: UART receiver
summary: Receives serial bytes, sampling in the middle of each bit and reporting bad frames.
how: Two flip-flops synchronize the incoming line.
After the start edge it waits half a bit, then samples once per bit time.
Short glitches are ignored, and a bad stop bit raises frame_error.
try: Connect it to uart_tx (tx to rx) and write a testbench that echoes bytes.
expect: PASS: uart_rx, 51 bytes received, glitch ignored, 1 frame error caught

title: SPI master
summary: Talks to sensors, flash memory and displays over SPI (mode 0).
how: cs_n goes low to select the device.
Data is read on the rising edge of sclk and changed on the falling edge, most significant bit first.
Sending and receiving happen at the same time.
try: Make the transfer width a parameter (8, 16 or 32 bits).
